# Changelog

All notable changes to Nexus Code are documented in this file.
The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.0.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

Detailed per-release documentation is maintained in [`docs/releases/`](docs/releases/).

## [Unreleased]

Inventory of work already on `release/v1.3.0` toward v1.3.0 (version strings still 1.2.2). Full unit table and open gaps: [`docs/releases/v1.3.0-READINESS.md`](docs/releases/v1.3.0-READINESS.md). External qualification pending; not a frontier-grade claim.

### Added
- Workspace manifest plugins (HK-3): a directory `.nexus/plugins/<name>/` with a `nexus-plugin.json` contributes command hooks that run as subprocesses under the project-hook rules. Approved per plugin by its tree digest with `nexus plugins trust <dir>`; any change to the tree asks again; managed policy and workspace trust stand above the approval. Skills a manifest names are recorded and not loaded. `docs/PLUGINS.md`.
- Client protocol schemas and docs (PF-1), `nexus run --json` result contract (PF-2).
- ACP adapter and conformance fixtures against Zed and CodeCompanion (AC-1, AC-2).
- `nexus verify`, MCP/ACP verify surfaces, sandbox-denial receipt records (VR-1, VR-2, VR-3).
- Managed policy tiers, audit export/verify, flight hash chain, telemetry transparency and opt-out, admin strict mode and allowlists (GV-1–GV-5).
- LSP lifecycle, bounds, position encodings and project roots (LS-1, LS-2).
- Experimental detached jobs: a supervised Linux runner, isolated worktrees, unattended policy, bounded budgets, receipts, recovery, and operator commands (BG-1).
- Experimental unattended schedules (BG-2): `nexus schedule add|list|status|remove|pause|resume|run-now` with `--cron`, `--every` and `--at` (UTC); the runner starts each run as an unattended job through the same path as `nexus job start`. A schedule needs a trusted workspace, fixes its permission level when added and is a path the agent's file tools refuse; missed runs are counted and reported (an optional single catch-up job with `--on-missed run-once`, never a burst), overlapping runs are skipped and recorded, and a clock stepped backwards never runs a slot twice. The job receipt gains `sch
- CI CLI-suite shard fan-out under stable required check names.
- Experimental unix-socket transport for the sidecar (PF-3): `sidecar.js --listen` binds a socket (mode 0600) in a private 0700 directory and prints its path on one stdout line; other clients attach with a per-start random token from a 0600 descriptor file, as one controller or as read-only observers, and may detach and attach again. A wrong, missing or late token is refused with one fixed line before any command is parsed. No client can grant allow-always or change the mode over the socket, and `--listen` is refused under auto approval. No TCP, HTTP or WebSocket listener. Protocol stays 1 (ne
- Command hooks (HK-1): `pre-tool` and `post-tool` programs declared in `~/.config/nexus/hooks.json` or an approved `<workspace>/.nexus/hooks.json`; a hook can deny a tool call and can never approve one or change its input. Approving project hooks needs a person at a terminal and covers the workspace scripts the hooks run. `nexus hooks list|approve|revoke|test`, a `hooks.config` doctor finding, `docs/HOOKS.md`.

### Fixed
- PA-3 goal semantics now meet their acceptance: a goal counts as driven only when its recorded driver (pid, host, kernel start time, boot id) names a live process on this host; a dead process, reused pid, other host or boot, or an incomplete record resumes `PAUSED` with a specific reason on the read path (`/goal status|list`, `nexus operation status`) and the drive path alike. Records from builds before `activeStartTicks` read as unknown identity and pause. The task-state directory is a protected path for the agent's file tools (real-path spelling, and hard links to any file below it). `--san
- BG-2 schedule recovery after a crash between job submit and schedule update: restore `lastFire`, decrement `remainingRuns`, and disable at zero so `--max-runs 1` cannot fire again; treat an in-flight job for the same slot as recovery, not overlap.

### Changed
- **Behaviour change, workspace plugins (HK-3).** A JavaScript plugin in a workspace's `.nexus/plugins/` or `plugins/` is loaded only when that file's exact bytes were approved with `nexus plugins trust <file>` (in a terminal); trusting the workspace no longer loads plugins by itself, and nothing is approved automatically on upgrade. An approved plugin runs from a private copy of its one file, so imports of sibling files and of the workspace's packages no longer resolve; such a plugin is reported as `load-failed` instead of being skipped silently. A workspace plugin cannot take the name of one
- Parallel resource admission for operations (PA-1 partial); staged PA-4 workflow surfaces as documented under `docs/v1.3.0/`.

### Not yet in Unreleased (still open on the plan)
- PF-3 (UDS transport), HK-2 (plugins) and the other hook events of HK-1, PA-2 and remaining PA-1/PA-4 items. Context-maturity and WP-P10-02 remain Codex-owned.

## [v1.2.2] - 2026-11-21

### Changed
- VC-8: the implementer and tester roles are refused the tools that reach outside the task. Both lose the browser tools and `manage_knowledge`; the tester also loses `fetch_web`, `search_web` and `spawn_subagent`. The agent neither offers a refused tool nor runs it when the model calls it anyway; the denial names the role and says why. Editing, testing, shell, git, LSP and objective tools are unchanged, and the path guards, verifier and review remain the controls for what they may change. Owner choice: network and side-channel tools (2026-11-21).
- Redaction variants (MT-3, part 2): `formatSafeSidecarText` calls the shared `safeTerminal` instead of restating it, with output byte-identical; the remaining variants are kept and each has a reason in `docs/v1.2.1/REDACTION_VARIANTS.md`. New `cli/test/mt3_redaction_characterization.test.ts` pins the exact output of 23 redaction and terminal-safe variants over a shared corpus.

### Added
- VC-9 (the two remaining cases): in `nexus run`, a requirement the model marks blocked now ends the run `BLOCKED / NEEDS_INPUT` (`kind: blocked_requirement`) with the blocker as the question, answered in free text with `--answer <id>=reply:<text>`; before it ended `COMPLETED / REQUIREMENTS_INCOMPLETE` with the reason only in a note (other surfaces are unchanged; the task status for this case is now `failed`, exit code still 1). Steering that would drop a requirement and got no decision before its turn ended now ends that turn `BLOCKED / NEEDS_INPUT` (`kind: steering_conflict`) and can be deci
- CS-10 (Docker and phase 2): on Linux, `--sandbox docker` now runs the native worker inside the hardened container as well (before, Docker confined commands only and the worker kept the operator's access). The worker is mounted read-only with the loader and libraries it was linked against in a private directory, so it starts in the pinned Alpine image without changing the image; its commands run in that container with the image's `sh`, as they did. `--sandbox docker` fails closed when the container cannot be built; plain `--sandbox` tries Bubblewrap, then Docker. Whenever the worker is sandbo
- Significant independent reviews now require eight non-empty engineering-assessment fields when a diff touches core code, five or more files, or at least 300 added/removed lines. The parser derives significance from the diff, fails closed on malformed or incomplete assessments, and never lets the assessment override verifier, scope, boundary, defect, or unproven-criteria rejection. This records review evidence; it does not prove the model's assessment is correct or independent.
- CS-9: operator command rules in `~/.config/nexus/command_rules.json` (operator home only; a project file is never read). Prefix rules decide a shell command as `allow` (no prompt in review mode), `prompt` (asks even in auto mode, unless `--yes`) or `forbidden` (refused in every mode); the strictest rule wins. `allow` needs every part of a chained command to match and no shell-active character; `prompt` and `forbidden` match any part. `match` and `notMatch` examples are checked when the file loads and a contradicting one rejects the whole file (reported once; the normal policy applies). The d
- VC-2: an authorised regression obligation is discharged only when the verifier output reports a recognised result for that exact test. A green suite that does not show the test, a skipped result, and older pass records without test-name binding remain unresolved and block completion.
- CS-11: a command that fails with only volatile text changing (a retry counter, request or job number, ephemeral port, temp directory name, counter after a transfer verb, compound duration; an HTTP status, a build step index and outcome counts stay distinct) is now the same failure to the non-progress tracker and to CS-3: it is noted and, with continuation on, stopped, instead of running to the step limit. The volatile-text patterns are anchored to a context word or unit, never to a bare number, and were measured on a new 86-pair labelled corpus (`cli/test/fixtures/volatile_text_corpus.json`)
- VC-9: a delegated subagent's headless decision (tool approval, verification-file edit, verifier approval) is no longer lost. The subagent stops at it and returns the question (same id and shape, plus `subagent: { depth, objective }`) to its parent, whose headless run ends BLOCKED / NEEDS_INPUT; `--answer` resumes it (the re-spawned subagent receives the answers). Further questions raised in the same turn are listed in `furtherNeedsInput`. The subagent itself still never approves. Interactive runs and top-level behaviour are unchanged. The child is spawned again on resume, not resumed. The re

### Fixed
- A failing type-check whose output is coloured is `FAILED`, not `ENVIRONMENT`. With `FORCE_COLOR=1` in the operator's environment `tsc` wraps the file, line and column in escape sequences; the diagnostics parser then located no file and the check was classified "could not run", which does not block completion (VC-6, CG-4). Escape sequences are removed before parsing.
- A native worker that exits right after launch (for example a Docker worker whose container fails to start) no longer raises an uncaught `EPIPE` that ended the CLI: the worker's stdin stream has an error listener and the waiting request is answered as a disconnect.
- Saving progress no longer fails on a worktree binding left over from an earlier turn ("Task state worktree path has no selected workspace identity"); it showed only when the workspace directory name tripped the secret classifier's high-entropy check.
- VC-6: Cargo projects are part of the pre-change type-check baseline (the per-workspace target directory is reused, so dependencies are not built twice); a regression case covers a pre-existing Rust diagnostic against a new one in an untouched caller.
- MCP and plugin tools now run. They were offered to the model but never registered in the capability registry, so the execution spine answered every call with `FAIL-001: Tool ... is not registered`; the server never received `tools/call`. They are now registered after connection as `extension` capabilities with conservative defaults: mutating (read-only sessions refuse them), `egress` for a remote server and `exec` for a local process or plugin (review mode asks first), and only local ones count as changing the workspace. Reproduced against a local MCP server first (`cli/test/mcp_tool_through
- The real language-server job's Rust setup: rust-analyzer is now added to the default toolchain (the product launches servers outside the repository, where the repository's pinned toolchain does not apply), and the test's availability probe runs in the fixture directory, as the product does.

### Fixed
- `lsp_diagnostics` for Rust no longer reports a file with type errors as clean: rust-analyzer sends an empty first `publishDiagnostics` before it has loaded the Cargo project and analysed types, and the client returned on it. Servers that analyse in stages are marked `awaitProgress` (rust-analyzer is); the client now advertises work-done progress, answers the server's own requests (`window/workDoneProgress/create`, `workspace/configuration`, ...), and waits for the server's progress to end (within the caller's timeout) before trusting a list.

### Changed
- The weekly real language-server job requires typescript, python and go (all three passed on the first hosted run); the rust-analyzer case still runs but reports as a todo, because the product could not start rust-analyzer on the runner although its `--version` probe passed (cause undiagnosed).

### Added
- Behavioural differential against a declared reference (plan unit VC-3, rest): `/requirements differential <R> --inputs <file>` runs the objective's latest verifier command and the operator-authorised reference command on each input (a JSON array of at most 50 strings, each at most 64 KiB) in the sandbox without network (30 s per run, output capped at 1 MiB), compares normalised output and exit code, and reports "run: N agree, M diverge" with the first differing line per divergence. A timed-out, errored or over-cap run is inconclusive, not agreement. Agreement on tested inputs is not equivale
- Real language servers (CS-6): `cli/test/lsp_real_servers.test.ts` runs the product's LSP client against typescript-language-server, pyright, rust-analyzer and gopls on a tiny fixture project (a deliberate error is reported; a clean file is a real empty report, not `unavailable`), skipping a server that is not installed unless `NEXUS_LSP_REQUIRE` names it. A weekly, non-required `lsp-real-servers` workflow installs the servers and requires TypeScript and Python. Not yet run on a hosted runner. See `docs/LSP_REAL_SERVERS.md`.

### Fixed
- `lsp_diagnostics`, `lsp_hover` and `lsp_definition` never worked for TypeScript, JavaScript or Python files: the default commands started `typescript-language-server` and `pyright-langserver` without `--stdio`, so both exited at once and every query was `unavailable`. Found by the real-server test (CS-6).

### Fixed
- The nightly real-project smoke (MQ-3) failed on its first hosted run on the pytest repository: the workflow installed pytest with `pip install --user`, the smoke runs the CLI under a throwaway `HOME`, and the verifier could not import it, while the script's own pytest probe ran under the real home and said it was available. The probe now runs under an isolated home (and says to install system-wide), and the workflow installs pytest system-wide.

### Changed
- The verifier convergence stop (DV-2: a stalled, oscillating or diverging failure history ends the turn BLOCKED with the attempt history) is now also judged when a verifier command is run through `run_tests` (or `run_command`), not only when the model calls `task_completed` (VC-7). A loop that only edits and re-runs the tests no longer waits for the step limit. A failure that changes each time, or a re-run on unchanged files, does not trip it.

### Added
- `scripts/gateway_conformance.mjs` and `docs/GATEWAY_CONFORMANCE.md` (MQ-4): a scheduled gateway conformance job for a local scheduler. It takes the `GATEWAY` claim without waiting (a held claim skips the run, exit 75), runs the unmodified tool-call matrix, judges each alias's native-valid ratio against the 99.5% bar and a baseline, and alerts (alert file and an operator command) on a drop, a run that produces nothing, or an alias below the bar; the claim is released on every exit path. Tested through the script with a fake runner; not yet run against the live gateway, and nothing is schedule

Command hooks that run before and after tool calls (they can deny a call, never

Options:

                          whether they are in force

  revoke [options]        Withdraw the approval of this workspace's

  test [options] <event>  Run the hooks in force against a sample tool call and
                          print what they decide (the tool itself is not run)
  help [command]          display help for command

  revoke [options] <id>  Withdraw the approval of a trigger in this workspace

  remove <name>                  Remove an installed plugin package by name

Convergence-scheduled multi-unit operations (reroute, park, wait, resume)

Options:
  -h, --help                                 display help for command

Commands:
  validate [options] <spec>                  Validate an operation spec without starting work
  run [options] <spec>                       Start an operation from a work-unit spec
  resume [options] [id]                      Resume an operation from durable state (after a restart, the wait continues or re-evaluates if overdue)
  decide [options] <id> <decision> <option>  Apply an operator decision to a blocked unit, then resume the operation
  status [options] [id]                      Show operation state, parked work, wake time and pending decisions
  budget [options] <id>                      Operator command: change an operation's token cap (audited in its journal; applies from the next dispatch)
  message [options] <id>                     Publish a typed message to an operation's work units
  checkpoint [options] <id> <unit>           Snapshot a settled unit's conversation so it can be restored later
  checkpoints [options] <id>                 List the operation's context checkpoints
  restore [options] <id> <unit> <name>       Restore a unit's conversation from a checkpoint (verification restarts fail-closed)

Usage: nexus audit [options] [command]

Inspect tool execution audit log and execution metrics

Options:

                                 "25")
  -t, --tool <name>              Filter by tool name
  --errors                       Show only failed executions
  -h, --help                     display help for command

Commands:
  export [options] <id>          Write the evidence of one task or session as a
                                 secret-redacted (not confidential) audit bundle

[experimental] Unattended schedules that start background jobs (see

# Tool registry

A tool is one registered pair: a **spec** (what the model sees and what the tool may affect) and a **binding** (how a call of it runs). Everything that needs to know about tools reads one `ToolRegistry` (`cli/src/core/tool_registry.ts`): the model-visible list, the route a call takes through the exe

## Add a tool

1. Write the spec as a `CanonicalCapability` in `cli/src/core/capability_definitions/` and add it to `BASELINE_CAPABILITIES` (`core/capabilities.ts`). The spec fixes `effect` (`read_workspace`, `write_workspace`, `exec`, `egress`, `delegate`, `context_inject`, `internal`), `mutating`, `changesWorksp
2. Give it a binding in `createToolRegistry`:
   - `native`: runs in-process. Pass `handler` in the binding, or register it on the spine in `setupSpineHandlers` (`core/spine_handlers.ts`).
   - `bridge`: runs in the Rust core through `RustCoreBridge.executeTool`. A spec with the `rust_rpc` backend is bridged without further work.
   - `extension`: MCP and plugin tools only. The agent registers them as they connect; do not register one by hand.
3. Choose an `offer` rule: when the model is offered the tool (`group`, `skills`, `always`, `objective`, `requirements`, `mask`, `until-all-groups`). A tool in a tool group (`core/tool_groups.ts`) uses `group`.
4. If `nexus serve-mcp` must not list it because it needs the model loop, set `agentBound`.

That is all: the model-visible list, the dispatch route, the parser's known names and the serve-mcp list follow. Run `tool_registry`, `tool_surface_characterization` and `tool_dispatch_characterization`; the last two are golden files that change on purpose when the catalogue grows (see `cli/test/hel

```ts
const registry = new ToolRegistry();
registry.register({
  spec,                                          // a CanonicalCapability
  binding: { kind: "native", handler },          // how a call runs
  offer: "group",
  baseline: true,                                // part of the derived lists
});
```

## What registration refuses

`register` throws, and registers nothing, for:

- a name that is already registered;
- a spec that carries its own `handler` next to a binding (a tool has one source for how it runs);
- a spec without a binding;
- an extension whose effect is not `exec` or `egress`. An extension therefore cannot register as `read_workspace` or `internal`, which never ask the operator; and the extension category, backend and binding must agree.

## What the registry does not do

It has no member that lowers an effect, marks a tool approval-free, or overrides the operator decision. Whether a call is asked, denied or run is decided in dispatch (`core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`) from the registered effect, the mode and the policy, as before. `tool_registry.test.ts` asserts the exp

# Tool registry

A tool is one registered pair: a **spec** (what the model sees and what the tool may affect) and a **binding** (how a call of it runs). Everything that needs to know about tools reads one `ToolRegistry` (`cli/src/core/tool_registry.ts`): the model-visible list, the route a call takes through the exe

## Add a tool

1. Write the spec as a `CanonicalCapability` in `cli/src/core/capability_definitions/` and add it to `BASELINE_CAPABILITIES` (`core/capabilities.ts`). The spec fixes `effect` (`read_workspace`, `write_workspace`, `exec`, `egress`, `delegate`, `context_inject`, `internal`), `mutating`, `changesWorksp
2. Give it a binding in `createToolRegistry`:
   - `native`: runs in-process. Pass `handler` in the binding, or register it on the spine in `setupSpineHandlers` (`core/spine_handlers.ts`).
   - `bridge`: runs in the Rust core through `RustCoreBridge.executeTool`. A spec with the `rust_rpc` backend is bridged without further work.
   - `extension`: MCP and plugin tools only. The agent registers them as they connect; do not register one by hand.
3. Choose an `offer` rule: when the model is offered the tool (`group`, `skills`, `always`, `objective`, `requirements`, `mask`, `until-all-groups`). A tool in a tool group (`core/tool_groups.ts`) uses `group`.
4. If `nexus serve-mcp` must not list it because it needs the model loop, set `agentBound`.

That is all: the model-visible list, the dispatch route, the parser's known names and the serve-mcp list follow. Run `tool_registry`, `tool_surface_characterization` and `tool_dispatch_characterization`; the last two are golden files that change on purpose when the catalogue grows (see `cli/test/hel

```ts
const registry = new ToolRegistry();
registry.register({
  spec,                                          // a CanonicalCapability
  binding: { kind: "native", handler },          // how a call runs
  offer: "group",
  baseline: true,                                // part of the derived lists
});
```

## What registration refuses

`register` throws, and registers nothing, for:

- a name that is already registered;
- a spec that carries its own `handler` next to a binding (a tool has one source for how it runs);
- a spec without a binding;
- an extension whose effect is not `exec` or `egress`. An extension therefore cannot register as `read_workspace` or `internal`, which never ask the operator; and the extension category, backend and binding must agree.

## What the registry does not do

It has no member that lowers an effect, marks a tool approval-free, or overrides the operator decision. Whether a call is asked, denied or run is decided in dispatch (`core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`) from the registered effect, the mode and the policy, as before. `tool_registry.test.ts` asserts the exp

## [Unreleased]

Inventory of work already on `release/v1.3.0` toward v1.3.0 (version strings still 1.2.2). Full unit table and open gaps: [`docs/releases/v1.3.0-READINESS.md`](docs/releases/v1.3.0-READINESS.md). External qualification p
ending; not a frontier-grade claim.

### Added
- Workspace manifest plugins (HK-3): a directory `.nexus/plugins/<name>/` with a `nexus-plugin.json` contributes command hooks that run as subprocesses under the project-hook rules. Approved per plugin by its tree digest
 with `nexus plugins trust <dir>`; any change to the tree asks again; managed policy and workspace trust stand above the approval. Skills a manifest names are recorded and not loaded. `docs/PLUGINS.md`.
- Client protocol schemas and docs (PF-1), `nexus run --json` result contract (PF-2).
- ACP adapter and conformance fixtures against Zed and CodeCompanion (AC-1, AC-2).
- `nexus verify`, MCP/ACP verify surfaces, sandbox-denial receipt records (VR-1, VR-2, VR-3).
- Managed policy tiers, audit export/verify, flight hash chain, telemetry transparency and opt-out, admin strict mode and allowlists (GV-1–GV-5).
- LSP lifecycle, bounds, position encodings and project roots (LS-1, LS-2).
- Experimental detached jobs: a supervised Linux runner, isolated worktrees, unattended policy, bounded budgets, receipts, recovery, and operator commands (BG-1).
- Experimental unattended schedules (BG-2): `nexus schedule add|list|status|remove|pause|resume|run-now` with `--cron`, `--every` and `--at` (UTC); the runner starts each run as an unattended job through the same path as
 `nexus job start`. A schedule needs a trusted workspace, fixes its permission level when added and is a path the agent's file tools refuse; missed runs are counted and reported (an optional single catch-up job with `--o
n-missed run-once`, never a burst), overlapping runs are skipped and recorded, and a clock stepped backwards never runs a slot twice. The job receipt gains `schedule_occurrence` and a filled-in `missed` (additive, versio
n 1); new schedule file schema `docs/protocol/schedule-v1.schema.json` and [`docs/SCHEDULES.md`](docs/SCHEDULES.md).
- CI CLI-suite shard fan-out under stable required check names.
- Experimental unix-socket transport for the sidecar (PF-3): `sidecar.js --listen` binds a socket (mode 0600) in a private 0700 directory and prints its path on one stdout line; other clients attach with a per-start rand
om token from a 0600 descriptor file, as one controller or as read-only observers, and may detach and attach again. A wrong, missing or late token is refused with one fixed line before any command is parsed. No client ca
n grant allow-always or change the mode over the socket, and `--listen` is refused under auto approval. No TCP, HTTP or WebSocket listener. Protocol stays 1 (new error codes `UNAUTHORIZED`, `NOT_CONTROLLER`, `NOT_PERMITT
ED`); `docs/PROTOCOL.md` "Socket transport", `examples/attach/`.
- Command hooks (HK-1): `pre-tool` and `post-tool` programs declared in `~/.config/nexus/hooks.json` or an approved `<workspace>/.nexus/hooks.json`; a hook can deny a tool call and can never approve one or change its inp
ut. Approving project hooks needs a person at a terminal and covers the workspace scripts the hooks run. `nexus hooks list|approve|revoke|test`, a `hooks.config` doctor finding, `docs/HOOKS.md`.

### Fixed
- PA-3 goal semantics now meet their acceptance: a goal counts as driven only when its recorded driver (pid, host, kernel start time, boot id) names a live process on this host; a dead process, reused pid, other host or 
boot, or an incomplete record resumes `PAUSED` with a specific reason on the read path (`/goal status|list`, `nexus operation status`) and the drive path alike. Records from builds before `activeStartTicks` read as unkno
wn identity and pause. The task-state directory is a protected path for the agent's file tools (real-path spelling, and hard links to any file below it). `--sandbox` (bwrap and Docker) masks the whole state root, creatin
g it first, and pins the directories between the workspace and the root so none can be renamed, even when the workspace is `$HOME` or its parent; a state path through a symlink inside the workspace, or a workspace that i
s the state directory, is refused with an explicit error. The advisory command check does not cover the directory. Fingerprint stalls compare the redacted form, so a secret-shaped failure reason now stalls. New `nexus op
eration budget <id> --max-total-tokens <n|none>` changes the token cap with a journal entry. `/team` and `nexus operation` leave experimental.
- BG-2 schedule recovery after a crash between job submit and schedule update: restore `lastFire`, decrement `remainingRuns`, and disable at zero so `--max-runs 1` cannot fire again; treat an in-flight job for the same s
lot as recovery, not overlap.

### Changed
- **Behaviour change, workspace plugins (HK-3).** A JavaScript plugin in a workspace's `.nexus/plugins/` or `plugins/` is loaded only when that file's exact bytes were approved with `nexus plugins trust <file>` (in a ter
minal); trusting the workspace no longer loads plugins by itself, and nothing is approved automatically on upgrade. An approved plugin runs from a private copy of its one file, so imports of sibling files and of the work
space's packages no longer resolve; such a plugin is reported as `load-failed` instead of being skipped silently. A workspace plugin cannot take the name of one of your own plugins. Your own plugin directories (`~/.nexus
/plugins/`, `~/.config/nexus/plugins/`) are not loaded when Nexus is started in a directory that contains them (your home directory), and the agent's file tools refuse them everywhere. The first session prints one notice
 listing the files that wait for approval; `nexus doctor` warns as `plugins.workspace`. Migration: `docs/PLUGINS.md`.
- Parallel resource admission for operations (PA-1 partial); staged PA-4 workflow surfaces as documented under `docs/v1.3.0/`.

### Not yet in Unreleased (still open on the plan)
- PF-3 (UDS transport), HK-2 (plugins) and the other hook events of HK-1, PA-2 and remaining PA-1/PA-4 items. Context-maturity and WP-P10-02 remain Codex-owned.

**Second independent review at `f25030a3c0c0cc64e5abbefadad06c648a9b59c4` — ACCEPT WITH FOLLOW-UPS. The PR merged at `8f5feae2` before these were addressed (the two later commits change one test line and the evidence doc), so they are open on `release/v1.3.0`.**
No blocker was found: extra or forged members on `_nexus/verify` are refused before anything runs, `$/cancel_request` aborts the worker and replies once, `close()` aborts and awaits a verification, read-only and the auto-approval refusal hold, the v1 ACP schema is untouched, and receipt lookup is bound to the session.
**Open follow-ups, in order of weight**
1. **A new session re-pins the base** (`cli/src/acp_stdio.ts`, `startSession`, about line 229). The base is pinned for every new or loaded session. A client can commit weakened tests, open a new session on the same directory, and be judged against a base that already contains them. The pin protects one session only. Either pin once per workspace for the life of the `nexus acp` process, or say plainly in `docs/ACP.md` and `docs/evidence/v1.3.0/VR2.md` that each new session re-pins.
2. **The client chooses the tree that is verified.** A verification covers the session's `cwd`, which the client picks; the operator's verifier command and deliverable list are fixed at start-up but applied to that directory (deliverables are normalised against the launch workspace, `config.ts:529`, then resolved against the session cwd). The receipt records `workspace` and `base_pinned_at`, but the `_nexus/verify` result does not name the workspace. Add it to the result and document the behaviour.
3. **Id-less `_nexus/receipt/get` can return a verification receipt** (confirmed by running; `latestReceipts`, about lines 353 and 418). The plan said id-less get keeps returning turn receipts only, so existing clients see no change. The test near `acp_stdio.test.ts:118` asserts the mixed behaviour.
4. **Interlocks are untested.** Removing the "no verify during a prompt" check leaves `acp_stdio` (9/9) and `acp_review_fixes` (8/8) green. There is no test for verify during a prompt or a stopping turn, a prompt during a verify, or read-only refusal over ACP; the cross-session receipt test (about line 125) uses a session id that is not active.
5. **Shutdown bound.** `ACP_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS` (10 s) equals the verify kill grace, so on a signal the process can exit before the worker has removed its scratch trees. `serve-mcp` allows 15 s. By reading only.
6. `_meta` is accepted on `_nexus/verify` and ignored; the docs say nothing else is accepted.
**Mutations run:** accepting an extra param fails `acp_stdio` and `acp_validate`; dropping the receipt's session binding fails `acp_stdio` and `verify_service`; allowing verify during a prompt fails nothing (item 4).
**Tests at `f25030a3`, 0 failures:** `acp_stdio` 9, `acp_validate` 15, `acp_schema` 7, `acp_mapping` 22, `acp_review_fixes` 8, `acp_client_conformance` 2, `verify_service` 10, `mcp_verify` 7, `mcp` 4.
**Not checked:** the real adapter over stdio with a real worker, SIGTERM of `nexus acp` during a live verification, two verifications on two sessions, Node 22.

===== 778
**Independent review at `afb4ed64f62d4b597eb75286e3fb92209ad367fb` — ACCEPT WITH FOLLOW-UPS. This merged before the review reported, so the follow-ups are against the release branch.**
**Follow-ups, in order of weight**
1. **A bare-name `mcp.allow` entry is not a boundary against a workspace file** (confirmed by running). With `allow = ["files"]` and a trusted workspace, a `.mcp.json` that defines a server named `files` with a different `command` was started and that program ran (`permitsMcpServer`, `core/managed_policy.ts:820-839`; `policyDescriptor`, `mcp.ts:129-135`). The same holds for a WebSocket, HTTP or SSE URL under an allowed name. The document says a name entry is the only kind that admits a WebSocket server; it does not say that a name entry pins nothing and that the workspace can redefine the name. Either a name-only entry should not match a definition that comes from the workspace, or the document must say so and recommend `mcp.disable_workspace = true` or `command:` / `url:` entries. I am opening a follow-up for the first.
2. **`nexus policy check <file>` echoes parts of the file in its parse errors** (confirmed by running): the first token of line 1 as an "invalid key", and a value such as `allow = sk-…` as an "unsupported value". Pointed at an arbitrary readable file it prints fragments of it. The offending token should be truncated or left out.
3. **Not traced:** `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK` is read in `sandbox.ts` and not in `verifyFlagRefusal`, so whether the environment variable gives `nexus verify` network access under a policy that refuses `--sandbox-network` is open.
4. A hard link to a workspace file placed in the user configuration directory counts as a user file under `disable_workspace` (confirmed by running). A repository cannot create that link; a limit to document.
5. A `sha256:` plugin pin covers the entry file only, not the modules it imports. To document.
**Held up when run**
- Name tricks (case, trailing space, a Cyrillic look-alike, a zero-width space) are all refused.
- A configuration symlinked into the workspace, a symlinked parent directory, and a workspace symlink pointing out are all treated as workspace under `disable_workspace`.
- `addServer` and `addConnection` refuse an unlisted server and nothing is spawned. The ACP adapter validates and ignores `mcpServers`.
- A plugin symlinked from the user plugin directory into the workspace is not imported under `plugins.disable_workspace`; a `sha256:` mismatch refuses.
- "Always": the approval is clamped, `setApprovalMode("auto")` cannot enter auto under the policy, and the one flag that approves silently is now gated.
- `doctor --fix` leaves a broken `policy.toml` byte-identical. `policy check --json` stays valid JSON with exit 2 on an unreadable file.
**Mutations, each caught:** removing the gate on `loadAndConnect` (10 failures), on `addConnection` (1), on `addServer` (1), the plugin gate (5), making `verifyFlagRefusal` return nothing (10), making "always" stick (1).
**Tests at that head:** `managed_policy_allowlists` 18, `managed_policy_verify` 12, `policy_cli` 23, `managed_policy_enforcement` 113, `managed_policy_schema` 57, `managed_policy_always` 6, `mcp` 4, `mcp_tool_through_spine` 3, `approval_policy` 16, `leak_guard` 6, all passing; `tsc`, the complex

PA-3 review (#806, S6). `driveOperation` pauses an operation whose recorded driver is not provably alive, but two callers pass a `prepare` hook that turns PAUSED back into RUNNING before it runs: `cli/src/core/job_worker.ts` (resumed detached jobs) and `cli/src/loop.ts` (a loop re-driving its own iteration operation). For those operations the stale pause is therefore overridden with no further operator action. Goals are unaffected: `GoalOrchestrator.resume` is the only path that clears a goal's pause and it is an explicit operator command. Open question: should a job or loop resume require the operator to see the stale reason first (for example record it as an event and continue, or block the job)? Comments now state the exact behaviour; no behaviour changed in #806.
Found while reviewing PF-3 (#797). A containment test of the form `path.relative(base, p).startsWith("..")` treats a first path segment that merely begins with two dots (for example `..hid`) as outside the base. Whether that fails closed or open depends on which way the caller uses the answer; for 'is this path inside the workspace' used as a refusal it fails open, as the PF-3 socket directory case showed (a sandboxed command could read the token from `<workspace>/..hid`).

The correct test is `rel === ".." || rel.startsWith(".." + path.sep) || path.isAbsolute(rel)`. PF-3 fixes it in `sandbox.ts` (`isPathWithin`) and `sidecar.ts`. Other sites found by grep, not reviewed one by one: `browser.ts` 100, 120, 265; `core/authority.ts` 637, 657, 692; `core/candidate.ts` 1089; `core/observation_identity.ts` 70, 93; `lsp.ts` 406; `safe_fs.ts` 39; `security.ts` 797, 821, 1012; `skills.ts` 332; `tester.ts` 446; `workspace_trust.ts` 39; `worktrunk/copy.ts` 58; `worktrunk/paths.ts` 122.

Proposed: one shared helper (reuse the exported `isPathWithin`), replace each site, and add a test per site with a `..x` file or directory. Not a v1.3.0 gate unless the review of a site shows a bypass.

# Unattended schedules

A schedule is a standing order to start a [detached job](RUNNER.md) at a time. The runner (`nexus runner serve`) fires it: each run is a normal unattended job in a fresh worktree, with every rule of `nexus job start`. A schedule decides **when**; it cannot ask for more than a job can. Experimental, Linux only, like the runner.

```sh
nexus trust /path/to/repo                       # once, after you have read the repository
nexus schedule add --name nightly --cron '0 3 * * 1-5' --prompt "Run the test suite and report failures" -w /path/to/repo
nexus schedule list
nexus schedule status nightly
nexus schedule run-now nightly                  # one run now; the schedule's grid is not touched
nexus schedule pause nightly                    # and: resume, remove (alias rm)
```

`add`, `list`, `status` and `run-now` take `--json` (`add` prints `{schedule, upcoming}`, `status` prints `{schedule, latest_job, last_fired_job, pointer, receipt}`). `add` also takes the job options (`--verifier`, `--deliverable-file`, the budget flags, `-e/-m/--provider`), `--max-runs N`, and `--on-missed report|run-once` (default `report`). There is no `--yes`, `--mode`, `--sandbox` or `--appro

## Triggers (all UTC)

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--cron '<m> <h> <dom> <mon> <dow>'` | Five fields: numbers, `*`, ranges `a-b`, steps `*/n` and `a-b/n`, lists. No names (`MON`), no `@daily`, no seconds, no `a/n`. Day-of-week `0` and `7` are Sunday. Slots must be at least 5 minutes apart, across midnight and month ends too, and an expression that never matches a date (`0 0 31 2 *`) is refused. When both day fields are restricted a day matches 
| `--every 15m` | Seconds, or `s`, `m`, `h`, `d`: from 5 minutes to 30 days. Slots are `created + k * interval`, so the phase never drifts. The first run is one interval after creation. |
| `--at 2026-12-01T03:00:00Z` | One run, then the schedule ends. UTC with the `Z`; a date that does not exist is refused. |

There is no time zone and so no daylight-saving change: a cron hour is a UTC hour, a day has 24 hours, and the clocks changing locally moves nothing. Leap seconds do not exist (Unix time); `0 0 29 2 *` runs on 29 February only, and an expression with no match in the next four years (`0 0 30 2 *`) is refused at `add`.

## What a schedule may ask for

The job a run starts is built by the same code as `nexus job start` (`core/job_submission.ts`), from the schedule's own record, so a fresh worktree from `HEAD` at the time of the run, the operator's verifier and deliverables, the unattended approval policy, bounded budgets, a deadline and bounded crash resumes all apply. Specifically:

- **Permission level, fixed when you add it.** `read-only` unless you pass `--allow-worktree-write`, which allows writes inside the run's own worktree only. Nothing the job does changes it. Managed policy applies as for a job: if it requires a human for workspace writes, `add` refuses `--allow-worktree-write`.
- **No auto mode, no allow-always.** A run never approves a command or a network call: it is denied at once and the run ends `BLOCKED` with the question in its receipt (`nexus operation decide ... --no-resume`, then `nexus job resume`). A denial remembers nothing, so the next identical request is denied too. The record has no field for a mode or a grant, and the reader refuses one.
- **Trusted workspaces only.** `add` refuses a repository `nexus trust` has not listed (the list the operator owns; `NEXUS_TRUST_WORKSPACE` is not consulted), and the runner checks the list again at every slot: a repository whose trust was withdrawn is refused and reported.
- **Same workspace.** The record holds the real path of the repository. A path that later resolves elsewhere (a swapped link) is refused.
- **The operator's verifier, and nothing else, runs without approval.** An unattended run approves no command, with one exception: the exact `--verifier` command you gave when you made the schedule. It runs in the sandbox, in the run's own worktree, gates completion, and managed `require_human` for commands still applies to it. Any other command (one the model names, one Nexus discovers in the rep
- **The verifier runs repository-controlled and model-written code without asking.** `node --test`, `npm test` and the like execute whatever the worktree holds: the repository's own files and anything the model wrote in the run, including a new test file it adds before calling the task done. Nothing prompts for that. What contains it: the run is sandboxed (no network, an empty fake HOME, writes st
- **A read-only run does not run its verifier.** A `read-only` run cannot change anything, so its completion is not gated and the verifier is not started. The receipt says so: `verifier.status` is `NOT_RUN` with the reason. Use `--allow-worktree-write` for a schedule whose point is a verified change.
- **The verifier string is yours, and a schedule file is a file.** A verifier runs without a prompt, so `add` and every fire hold it to what an interactive command is held to: one line of at most 2000 characters, not on the security policy's blocked-command list, not forbidden by your `command_rules.json`. A hand-edited record can name any verifier that passes those checks and it will then run in 

Not in v1.3.0: event triggers, SSH execution, wake checks, goal (objective-ledger) targets, time zones, schedule spec files (a repository cannot supply a schedule).

## Missed runs, overlap and the clock

A slot is **missed** when the runner could not serve it: it was not running, the host slept, or the clock jumped forward. A slot is on time when it is within 30 seconds of the runner looking at it.

- **Reported, never silent.** Every missed slot is counted. The runner writes one **gap** per catch-up: `count`, the `first` and `last` slot, the reason (`runner_not_running`, `overlap`, `refused`) in the schedule's record (the last 50 gaps), in `nexus schedule status` and `list`, in the runner log, and as a missed-run receipt `nexus-schedules/<id>.missed-<time>.json` (the last 20 are kept). A gap
- **Never replayed as a burst.** Late slots are never run one by one. With `--on-missed report` (the default), no catch-up job runs for a gap; the missed slots are recorded and reported. With `--on-missed run-once`, **one** catch-up job stands for the whole gap, for its last slot, and its receipt carries `missed: {count, first, last}` and `schedule_occurrence`. If the newest slot is on time, that 
- **Phase kept.** The next slot is always the next one on the schedule's own grid after now.
- **Overlap.** A slot that falls due while the schedule's previous job is still running starts nothing: it is recorded as an `overlap` gap (`last outcome SKIPPED_OVERLAP`). Two jobs of one schedule never run at once; `run-now` refuses while one runs.
- **A refusal is a miss too.** A run that cannot be submitted (untrusted workspace, queue full at 32 jobs, a repository that is not a repository, managed policy) is recorded as a `refused` gap with the reason and the schedule moves on.
- **Clock stepped backwards.** If the runner finds the clock more than two minutes behind where it was, it counts the step (`status` shows it) and recomputes the next slot from the clock as it is, so the schedule does not sleep until the old time returns. A slot that already has a job (same schedule, same `dueAt`) is never started again, so going back and forward over a slot runs it once. A forwar
- **A runner that dies after submitting** does not run the slot twice either: the job found for the slot is the run.
- **Pause and resume.** Time spent paused is not missed time; `resume` continues from the next slot after now. A `once` whose time has passed cannot be resumed.
- `--max-runs N` ends the schedule after N started runs. At most 64 schedules; the 65th `add` is refused, and files beyond 64 are reported and never run.

## Delivery

Each run's receipt is the job receipt (`schedule_id`, `schedule_occurrence`, `missed`, `unattended: true`). The runner also records the outcome in the schedule (`last outcome`) and writes `<id>.latest.json`, a pointer `{jobId, receipt, outcome, integrationBranch, at}`. Results stay on the job's integration branch; nothing is merged and nothing is written into your checkout.

- **Pause and resume.** Time spent paused is not missed time; `resume` continues from the next slot after now. A `once` whose time has passed cannot be resumed.

## Limits and residual risks

- An approved hook runs with your authority, outside the sandbox.
- A project's hooks (and a workspace plugin's) are a service the repository offers, not a control over the agent:
  the agent can edit `.nexus/hooks.json`, or a script it runs, like any other file. An edit takes the hooks out of
  force until you approve again; one notice says so (`WARNING: project hooks ... are NO LONGER IN FORCE`), once per
  session. Nothing unapproved runs, but the guard is gone. Put a guard you rely on in your own
  `~/.config/nexus/hooks.json`. That file is outside the workspace, where the file tools cannot write; a shell
  command that runs without the sandbox can still change it, like any file of yours, and a change that breaks the
  file denies every call instead of dropping the guard.
- The terminal check on `nexus hooks approve` stops a tool call that simply runs the command. It is not a boundary
  against a shell command that runs **outside the sandbox with your rights** (auto mode, sandbox off): such a command
  can fake a terminal (for example with `script`), or write `~/.config/nexus/extension_trust.json` directly. Nexus
  has no marker that tells a process it was started by the agent. Run the agent sandboxed, or keep approvals on, if
  the repository's content is not trusted.
- Hooks see the full arguments of every tool call they name.
- The approval store and the operator's hooks file are protected by file permissions only: another process running as
  you can change them.
- `nexus serve-mcp` has no hooks.
- Not in this version: other events (`pre-verify`, `post-verify`, `permission-request`, `session-start`,
  `session-end`, `stop`, `pre-compact`), hooks that change a tool's input, HTTP or prompt hooks, managed-policy keys
  for hooks.

The JSON Schema of the file, the input, the answer and the approval store is
[`docs/protocol/hooks-v1.schema.json`](protocol/hooks-v1.schema.json).

# Event triggers (BG-3)

Event triggers let a workspace declare that Nexus should start a run when an event fires. v1.3.0 ships the **trust
and abuse model** for triggers; the trigger firer itself (watching files and HTTP) is deferred to v1.4. Nothing runs
automatically until you approve it.

Two event kinds:

- **`file-change`** — run when files matching glob paths change. `paths` is required; `secret` must not be set.
- **`webhook`** — run when an HTTP webhook is delivered. `secret` is required to authenticate the caller; `paths` must not be set.

## Where triggers are declared

| File | Who writes it | When it runs |

| `<workspace>/.nexus/triggers.json` | the repository | only while its exact bytes are the ones you approved with `nexus triggers approve` |

# Agent Client Protocol

`nexus acp` serves the supported subset of ACP v1 over newline-delimited JSON-RPC on standard input and output. Standard
output is reserved for protocol messages. Diagnostics and model activity do not become JSON-RPC success responses.

The adapter runs each session through Nexus's existing `ApplicationCore` and `SidecarServer`, preserving workspace
policy, read-only restrictions, tool authorization, verification, and receipt generation. ACP clients cannot change the
operator's execution mode or policy. A permission response can approve one pending action only; rejecting, cancelling,
an unknown option, or a malformed response denies that action. A client cannot turn a policy refusal into an approval.

The adapter supports `initialize`, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, `session/cancel`, protocol request
cancellation, streamed messages and tool updates, client-bound permission requests, `_nexus/receipt/get`, and

**Where the interpreter is taken from.** Nexus resolves the name itself, to an absolute path, and starts that path.
  A bare name is looked up in the entries of `PATH` that are trusted directories, then in `/usr/local/bin`,
  `/usr/bin`, `/bin`, `/usr/sbin`, `/sbin`; an absolute path (`/usr/bin/python3`) must lie in a trusted directory. A
  directory is trusted when it is an absolute path, belongs to root or to you, cannot be written by group or others,
  and is not inside the workspace, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev` (so not `/dev/shm`), `/proc`, `/run` or `/sys`; the
  program itself must meet the same conditions. Empty and relative `PATH` entries (the current directory) are never
  used. An interpreter in a directory that your group can write (a `~/.local/bin` of mode 775, say) is therefore not
  found: `chmod g-w` the directory, or use the system's interpreter.

  **The `#!` line.** A script run directly (form 1) must begin with `#!` followed by the absolute path of one of
  the interpreters above in a trusted directory, and at most one of its options listed above: `#!/bin/sh`,
  `#!/bin/bash -eu`, `#!/usr/bin/python3 -I`. `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is refused (`env` finds the real program on
  `PATH`), and so is a relative path (`#!./tool` is looked up in the workspace). The line is read as the kernel reads
  it: only spaces and tabs separate, and a line with any other control character or a non-ASCII character is refused. For such a script use form 2,
  `["bash", "./guard.sh"]`: after an explicit shell, `node` or `python` the line is a comment and is not looked at.
  After `perl` or `ruby`, which act on the line themselves, it must be absent or follow the same rule.

  The script must be a regular file in the workspace. What follows it is passed to the script; an argument there (or
  the value of `--option=value` or `-ovalue`) that is an existing path in the workspace must be a regular file too.
- **Everything else is refused for a project file**, which is then invalid (not run, cannot be approved). That
  includes any other program, installed or not (`/usr/bin/true`, `awk`, `make`, `git`, `jq`, `npm run`, `npx`); every
  program that starts another (`env`, `nice`, `timeout`, `xargs`, `script`, `su`, `sudo`, `runuser`, `busybox`,
  `setsid`); other shells and interpreters (`ash`, `ksh`, `csh`, `fish`, `lua`, `Rscript`, `php`, `deno`, `bun`); any
  inline code or loader option (`-c`, `-e` for `node`, `-m`, `--eval`, `--require`, `--import`, `--run`, `--`); and a
  directory where the script should be (`node hookdir`). This is an allowlist: a form that is not listed above is
  refused whether or not anyone has thought of it. A hook that needs another program belongs in your own
  `~/.config/nexus/hooks.json`, which is not restricted this way.
- **The approval covers the script and the files given to it.** Each is recorded with its SHA-256 and shown by
  `nexus hooks list` and `approve`. If one changes, or the command comes to name another, the hooks stop on the next
  tool call and the notice names what changed, exactly as for the hooks file itself.
- **A project hook runs from the approved bytes, not from the workspace.** Just before a hook starts, each covered
  file is read once, those bytes are checked against the approval, and the same bytes are written to a private
  directory under `~/.nexus/hook-runs/` (owner-only; removed when the hook ends, and one that a killed run left
  behind is removed by a later run once it is ten minutes old). The command is started with those
  copies in place of the workspace paths, so a file replaced at that very moment cannot be what runs. The working
  directory is still the workspace. Consequences for a script:
  - it runs under a path outside the workspace, so `$0`, `__filename`, `__file__` and `dirname "$0"` do not lead back
    to the repository, and a file it looks for beside itself (`require("./lib")`, `import` of a sibling, a
    `package.json` that makes a `.js` file an ES module: use `.mjs` or `.cjs`) is not there;
  - **it must be one self-contained file.** A file it sources, imports or reads by a workspace path
    (`. ./lib.sh`, `cat rules.txt`) is taken from the workspace as it is at that moment and is **not** covered by the
    approval: anyone who can write the workspace can change it. Pass a data file as an argument to have it covered.
- What this does not cover: the files just named; the interpreter itself and the rest of the system, which are
  trusted as installed; and a process that already runs with your rights outside the sandbox, which can write
  `~/.nexus/hook-runs/` and the approval store directly.

## Migrating workspace plugins

**What changed.** Before v1.3.0, trusting a workspace (`nexus trust`) loaded every `*.js` and `*.mjs` file in its
plugin directories, with their sibling files and the workspace's packages in reach. From v1.3.0:

| Before | Now |
|---|---|
| `nexus trust` loads all workspace plugins | each plugin file also needs `nexus plugins trust <file>` |
| a changed plugin file is loaded as it is | a changed file is not loaded until approved again |
| a plugin may import sibling files and workspace packages | a plugin is one self-contained file |
| a plugin that fails to import is silently skipped | it is reported as `load-failed` with the reason |
| a workspace plugin can replace a plugin of yours with the same name | yours is used; the workspace's is `shadowed` |

**What stops loading after the upgrade.** Every workspace plugin, until you approve it. Nothing is approved for you.
The first session in such a workspace prints one notice that lists the files with the command for each:

```text
nexus: 2 workspace plugins are not loaded. Since v1.3.0 each workspace plugin file needs its own approval; trusting the workspace no longer loads them. Review each file, then run in a terminal:
  nexus plugins trust .nexus/plugins/audit.js
  nexus plugins trust plugins/format.mjs
```

`nexus doctor` reports the same as the warning `plugins.workspace`, and `nexus plugins list` shows each file's status.
A hook the plugin provided (a `preToolExecution` that refuses calls, say) is **not running** until then.

**What to do.**

1. Read each plugin file. Approve it with `nexus plugins trust <file>` in a terminal.
2. If the plugin imports sibling files or packages, it will show as `load-failed`. Make it one file (bundle it, or
   inline the helpers), then approve the new file.
3. Consider moving it out of the repository: a plugin in `~/.nexus/plugins/` is yours and needs no approval. What
   protects it: it lies outside the workspace, the agent's file tools refuse to read or write that directory in any
   workspace, and under the sandbox the agent's commands cannot reach it. What does not: a shell command that runs
   outside the sandbox with your rights can write there, as it can write any file of yours.
4. A plugin whose job is to refuse or log tool calls is better written as a command hook, which runs as a separate
   process and can only deny: see [`HOOKS.md`](HOOKS.md). `preToolExecution` that refuses maps to a `pre-tool` hook,

**Where the interpreter is taken from.** Nexus resolves the name itself, to an absolute path, and starts that path.
  A bare name is looked up in the entries of `PATH` that are trusted directories, then in `/usr/local/bin`,
  `/usr/bin`, `/bin`, `/usr/sbin`, `/sbin`; an absolute path (`/usr/bin/python3`) must lie in a trusted directory. A
  directory is trusted when it is an absolute path, belongs to root or to you, cannot be written by group or others,
  and is not inside the workspace, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev` (so not `/dev/shm`), `/proc`, `/run` or `/sys`; the
  program itself must meet the same conditions. Empty and relative `PATH` entries (the current directory) are never
  used. An interpreter in a directory that your group can write (a `~/.local/bin` of mode 775, say) is therefore not
  found: `chmod g-w` the directory, or use the system's interpreter.

  **The `#!` line.** A script run directly (form 1) must begin with `#!` followed by the absolute path of one of
  the interpreters above in a trusted directory, and at most one of its options listed above: `#!/bin/sh`,
  `#!/bin/bash -eu`, `#!/usr/bin/python3 -I`. `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is refused (`env` finds the real program on
  `PATH`), and so is a relative path (`#!./tool` is looked up in the workspace). The line is read as the kernel reads
  it: only spaces and tabs separate, and a line with any other control character or a non-ASCII character is refused. For such a script use form 2,
  `["bash", "./guard.sh"]`: after an explicit shell, `node` or `python` the line is a comment and is not looked at.
  After `perl` or `ruby`, which act on the line themselves, it must be absent or follow the same rule.

  The script must be a regular file in the workspace. What follows it is passed to the script; an argument there (or
  the value of `--option=value` or `-ovalue`) that is an existing path in the workspace must be a regular file too.
- **Everything else is refused for a project file**, which is then invalid (not run, cannot be approved). That
  includes any other program, installed or not (`/usr/bin/true`, `awk`, `make`, `git`, `jq`, `npm run`, `npx`); every
  program that starts another (`env`, `nice`, `timeout`, `xargs`, `script`, `su`, `sudo`, `runuser`, `busybox`,
  `setsid`); other shells and interpreters (`ash`, `ksh`, `csh`, `fish`, `lua`, `Rscript`, `php`, `deno`, `bun`); any
  inline code or loader option (`-c`, `-e` for `node`, `-m`, `--eval`, `--require`, `--import`, `--run`, `--`); and a
  directory where the script should be (`node hookdir`). This is an allowlist: a form that is not listed above is
  refused whether or not anyone has thought of it. A hook that needs another program belongs in your own
  `~/.config/nexus/hooks.json`, which is not restricted this way.
- **The approval covers the script and the files given to it.** Each is recorded with its SHA-256 and shown by
  `nexus hooks list` and `approve`. If one changes, or the command comes to name another, the hooks stop on the next
  tool call and the notice names what changed, exactly as for the hooks file itself.
- **A project hook runs from the approved bytes, not from the workspace.** Just before a hook starts, each covered
  file is read once, those bytes are checked against the approval, and the same bytes are written to a private
  directory under `~/.nexus/hook-runs/` (owner-only; removed when the hook ends, and one that a killed run left
  behind is removed by a later run once it is ten minutes old). The command is started with those
  copies in place of the workspace paths, so a file replaced at that very moment cannot be what runs. The working
  directory is still the workspace. Consequences for a script:
  - it runs under a path outside the workspace, so `$0`, `__filename`, `__file__` and `dirname "$0"` do not lead back
    to the repository, and a file it looks for beside itself (`require("./lib")`, `import` of a sibling, a
    `package.json` that makes a `.js` file an ES module: use `.mjs` or `.cjs`) is not there;
  - **it must be one self-contained file.** A file it sources, imports or reads by a workspace path
    (`. ./lib.sh`, `cat rules.txt`) is taken from the workspace as it is at that moment and is **not** covered by the
    approval: anyone who can write the workspace can change it. Pass a data file as an argument to have it covered.
- What this does not cover: the files just named; the interpreter itself and the rest of the system, which are
  trusted as installed; and a process that already runs with your rights outside the sandbox, which can write

**What changed.** Before v1.3.0, trusting a workspace (`nexus trust`) loaded every `*.js` and `*.mjs` file in its

|---|---|

## Documented limits (not defects, not closed)

- A command that runs **without a sandbox, with the operator's rights**, can fake a terminal (for example with `script`) and approve project hooks, workspace plugins and triggers, or write the approval store directly (`docs/HOOKS.md`, `docs/PLUGINS.md`, `docs/TRIGGERS.md`).
- Any other process running as the **same uid** can change the approval stores, the operator hooks file, goal state and runner state; protection there is file mode only.
- **Goal state is not signed.** Integrity rests on mode 0600 and the agent's file-tool refusals; an unsandboxed command can rewrite caps, stall counts and driver identity (`docs/v1.3.0/PA3_GOAL_LIFECYCLE.md`).
- Workspace JS plugins run in process with full process authority once approved; an absolute or dynamic load inside an approved entry is not covered (`docs/PLUGINS.md`).
- A `sha256:` plugin pin in policy covers the entry file only; a plugin file is hashed and then imported by path (`docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md`).
- Sandbox coverage: Bubblewrap on Linux and Docker; no kernel, seccomp or macOS/Windows layer is claimed. The sandbox hides the task-state root and the socket directory by mounts and pins, which were exercised on one host kernel with bwrap 0.13.1 and a local Docker daemon; other kernels, user-namespace settings and bwrap versions are unmeasured. Unattended jobs, schedules and the runner are Linux only.
- An unattended verifier the operator named runs repository-controlled and model-written code without a prompt, inside the sandbox (`docs/SCHEDULES.md`).
- A `--listen` socket is readable by an unsandboxed approved command that can read the descriptor file.
- Live inference is the project's gateway only; no gateway measurement for v1.3.0 exists in this record.

- **Goal state is not signed.** Integrity rests on mode 0600 and the agent's file-tool refusals; an unsandboxed command can rewrite caps, stall counts and driver identity (`docs/v1.3.0/PA3_GOAL_LIFECYCLE.md`).
- Workspace JS plugins run in process with full process authority once approved; an absolute or dynamic load inside an approved entry is not covered (`docs/PLUGINS.md`).
- A `sha256:` plugin pin in policy covers the entry file only; a plugin file is hashed and then imported by path (`docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md`).
- Sandbox coverage: Bubblewrap on Linux and Docker; no kernel, seccomp or macOS/Windows layer is claimed. The sandbox hides the task-state root and the socket directory by mounts and pins, which were exercised on one host kernel with bwrap 0.13.1 and a local Docker daemon; other kernels, user-namespace settings and bwrap versions are unmeasured. Unattended jobs, schedules and the runner are Linux only.
- An unattended verifier the operator named runs repository-controlled and model-written code without a prompt, inside the sandbox (`docs/SCHEDULES.md`).
- A `--listen` socket is readable by an unsandboxed approved command that can read the descriptor file.
- Live inference is the project's gateway only; no gateway measurement for v1.3.0 exists in this record.

**Draft.** Written against `origin/release/v1.3.0` tip `09eb0b12f` before any version bump. Nothing here is released, tagged or published; version strings are still 1.2.2. Replace the evidence SHAs and the "in flight" items at the RC commit.

**Maturity:** release candidate. Supersedes nothing; the previous stable release is [`v1.2.2`](v1.2.2.md). **External qualification is pending.** This is not a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade. Every test, review and measurement named here is internal validation, and results are reported as measured, including open findings. State of each gate and unit: [`v1.3.0-READINESS.md`](v1.3.0-READINESS.md) ("ledger closed for the landed units, qualification pending").

Theme (from [`docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`](../v1.3.0/PLAN.md)): let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate. Every new surface goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal. Experimental surfaces are marked experimental below and in their documents.

## What is new, by track

- **Protocol and embedding.** The sidecar protocol has generated JSON Schemas, a published document and version negotiation (PF-1, `docs/PROTOCOL.md`, #697 #700 #712). `nexus run --json` has a versioned result contract and documented exit codes (PF-2, #705). A library entry point and an embedding guide (PF-4, `docs/EMBEDDING.md`, #779 #786; not published to npm). Experimental: `sidecar.js --listen` accepts other clients on a private unix socket with a token, as controller or read-only observers (PF-3, #797).
- **IDE access.** `nexus acp` serves the supported subset of ACP v1 over stdio; client permission answers can approve one pending action and nothing else (AC-1, `docs/ACP.md`, #740 #741 #752). Conformance fixtures recorded from Zed 1.29.3 and CodeCompanion.nvim 20.3.0, no live model (AC-2, `docs/evidence/AC2_ACP_CONFORMANCE.md`, #749); those captures predate later ACP changes.
- **Verification layer.** `nexus verify` gives a verdict (VERIFIED, REGRESSION_FREE, UNVERIFIED, BLOCKED) on a change without running an agent (VR-1, #707). The same check is available to other harnesses through an MCP tool and ACP `_nexus/verify`; the caller cannot raise the verdict (VR-2, `docs/evidence/v1.3.0/VR2.md`, #756 #777). Sandbox denials are recorded as receipt and flight events and never raise a verdict (VR-3, #745).
- **Governance.** Managed policy with precedence system, user, project; restrict-only; a parse error in the system or user tier fails closed; `nexus policy show|check` (GV-1, `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md`, #717 #738 #778 #783). Admin strict mode and MCP/plugin allowlists (GV-5). `nexus audit export|verify` bundles with a hash manifest, optional ed25519 signing (GV-2, `docs/AUDIT.md`, #714 #771 #772). A hash-chained flight recorder checked on replay (GV-3, #696 #701 #761). Telemetry transparency and an opt-out (GV-4, `docs/TELEMETRY.md`, #695).
- **Hooks and plugins.** `pre-tool` and `post-tool` command hooks that can deny a call and never approve one (HK-1, `docs/HOOKS.md`, #782 #805). Plugin packages with a `nexus-plugin.json` manifest, installed from a local directory and verified against an install receipt: `nexus plugins install|list-installed|remove|verify` (HK-2, #796). Per-plugin approval for workspace plugins and workspace manifest plugins that run as subprocesses (HK-3, `docs/PLUGINS.md`, #798 #808 #810). Not in this candidate from the plan text: the other hook events, git-URL installs pinned to a commit, trigger-loaded skills (see Not in this release).
- **Background and scheduled runs (experimental, Linux).** A detached runner and `nexus job`/`nexus runner` (BG-1, `docs/RUNNER.md`, #780). `nexus schedule` with `--cron`, `--every`, `--at`, each run an unattended job in a fresh worktree (BG-2, `docs/SCHEDULES.md`, #799 #801 #802). Event-trigger trust model and `nexus triggers list|approve|revoke|status` (BG-3 trust model, `docs/TRIGGERS.md`, #803). **BG-3 firing (file watcher, signed webhooks): in flight as draft PR #812; not in this candidate unless it merges before the cut.**
- **Parallel agents and goals.** `nexus operation watch` and worktree owner receipts, resource admission (PA-1, #787 #794). Merge arbitration that re-verifies the merged tree (PA-2, #785 #788 #790). Goal semantics: a goal from a dead process resumes paused, fingerprint stall counting, completion only by a verifier receipt, an optional token budget (`nexus operation budget`) (PA-3, `docs/v1.3.0/PA3_ACCEPTANCE.md`, #758 #775 #789 #806 #809 #811). `/goal`, `/loop`, `/batch` and `/team` are in the command catalogue; `nexus operation validate` checks a spec (PA-4, staged, #709 #713 #793).
- **Sandbox and tools.** Named sandbox profiles `--sandbox :workspace|:read-only|:network` (SB-1, #781 #795; further slices in flight). One tool registry binds each spec to its handler (MT-2 slices 1-2, `docs/TOOL_REGISTRY.md`, #784 #804; later slices in flight).
- **Language servers and CI.** LSP lifecycle, bounds, position encodings and project roots (LS-1, LS-2, #718 #733 #736 #739 #751). CLI suite shard fan-out under stable required check names (#742 #743 #746 #748 #750).

## Behaviour changes that need a migration note

1. **Workspace JavaScript plugins need per-file approval (HK-3).** A plugin in a workspace's `.nexus/plugins/` or `plugins/` loads only when its exact bytes were approved with `nexus plugins trust <file>` in a terminal. `nexus trust` alone no longer loads it; nothing is approved on upgrade. An approved plugin runs from a private copy of its one file, so imports of sibling files or workspace packages fail and the plugin shows `load-failed`. A workspace plugin cannot take a name of your own plugin. Your own plugin directories (`~/.nexus/plugins/`, `~/.config/nexus/plugins/`) are not loaded when Nexus starts in a directory that contains them (your home). First session prints a notice; `nexus doctor` warns `plugins.workspace`. Migration table: `docs/PLUGINS.md` "Migrating workspace plugins". (#798 #808 #810)
2. **Project hooks accept only an allowlisted command shape and run from verified copies (HK-1).** A project's `.nexus/hooks.json` command must be one of the listed forms (an explicit interpreter with a workspace script, or a script with an absolute `#!` line); `env`, `npm run`, `make`, inline code (`-c`, `-e`), other launchers are refused and the file is invalid. Approval records SHA-256 of the script and the files given to it; the hook runs from a private copy of those bytes under `~/.nexus/hook-runs/`, so `$0`, sibling imports and sourced files do not lead back to the repository. Approving needs a person at a terminal. Hooks that need anything else belong in `~/.config/nexus/hooks.json`. (`docs/HOOKS.md`, #782 #805)
3. **A name in `mcp.allow` no longer admits a workspace-defined server (GV-1).** A bare name does not pin the command; a workspace `.mcp.json` entry of that name is refused. Use `command:` or `url:` entries or `mcp.disable_workspace = true` for a boundary. `nexus policy check <file>` validates a policy before rollout; exit code 2 means Nexus would refuse to start. (`docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md`, #778 #783)
4. **A broken system or user policy file fails closed.** Nexus refuses to start (exit 2) and names the file and tier. `/etc/nexus/policy.toml` is the system tier.
5. **Unattended jobs and schedules.** They never approve a command or a network call and have no allow-always; the only command that runs without approval is the exact operator `--verifier`, in the sandbox, in the run's worktree (it runs repository and model-written code without a prompt). A `read-only` run does not run its verifier and says so (`verifier.status: NOT_RUN`). A schedule needs a trusted workspace (`nexus trust`) that is checked again at every slot. (`docs/SCHEDULES.md`, `docs/RUNNER.md`, #780 #799 #802)
6. **Schedules are UTC with a 5-minute floor.** `--cron` and `--at` are UTC, `--every` is 5 minutes to 30 days, cron slots must be at least 5 minutes apart, there is no time zone and no `@daily`. Missed runs are counted and reported; `--on-missed report` (default) runs nothing, `run-once` runs one catch-up job. At most 64 schedules.
7. **`--listen` socket (experimental).** Refused under auto approval; the socket is mode 0600 in a 0700 directory; the token comes from a 0600 descriptor file; the sidecar refuses a socket directory inside the workspace; under `--sandbox` the directory is hidden from commands. A client cannot grant allow-always or change the mode. Protocol stays 1 (new error codes `UNAUTHORIZED`, `NOT_CONTROLLER`, `NOT_PERMITTED`). (`docs/PROTOCOL.md`, #797)
8. **Goal pause semantics (PA-3).** A goal whose recorded driver (pid, host, kernel start time, boot id) is not a live process on this host resumes `PAUSED` with a reason, on the read path and the drive path. Records from builds before `activeStartTicks` pause. The operation record schema is now v7. `/team` and `nexus operation` are no longer experimental. Known gap: an unattended job or loop `prepare` can override a stale pause (#807). (`docs/v1.3.0/PA3_GOAL_LIFECYCLE.md`)
9. **`--sandbox` masks the task-state directory and pins its ancestors.** A state path through a symlink inside the workspace, or a workspace that is the state directory, is refused with an explicit error (PA-3, #811). The agent's file tools refuse `~/.nexus/tasks`.
10. **Sandbox profiles (SB-1).** `--sandbox :read-only` sets the approval mode like `--read-only`; `:network` is an explicit network request that managed `sandbox.forbid_network` refuses; profiles apply with the other clamps and cannot loosen policy.
11. **Audit export refuses a repository whose own Git configuration names a program, and a workspace with a submodule,** instead of hashing it (`binding` becomes `unavailable`). (#772 #776)
12. **Budget flags.** Objective-wide tool-invocation and cumulative task-time limits exist (`--max-tool-invocations`, `--max-task-minutes`); an objective that exceeds them stops. (#699 #760 #774)
13. **BG-3 triggers.** When the firer lands, a workspace `.nexus/triggers.json` fires only while its exact bytes are approved with `nexus triggers approve`, runs read-only unattended jobs by default, and is rate-limited and quarantined; no trigger runs on upgrade. Until #812 merges, `nexus triggers` manages approvals only and nothing fires.

## Security notes and limits

- Nothing in this candidate is independent qualification. The review record (agent-run reviews posted as PR comments, with the defects they found and the follow-ups still open) is in the readiness inventory.
- A command that runs without a sandbox, with your rights, can fake a terminal and approve project hooks, workspace plugins and triggers, or write the approval stores. Run the agent sandboxed, or keep approvals on, for untrusted repositories.
- Any other process of the same user can change approval stores, goal state and runner state. Goal state is not signed.
- Workspace JS plugins run in process after approval; manifest plugins run as subprocesses with the project-hook rules.
- Sandbox: Bubblewrap and Docker only, exercised on one host kernel; no kernel-level or seccomp guarantee is claimed; other kernels and bwrap versions are unmeasured.
- A `--listen` socket and its descriptor are readable by an unsandboxed approved command.
- Open review follow-ups at the tip: #770 (process-tree sweep bound), #795 (network-state reset, doctor posture), #797 (bind-then-chmod window, `--listen` without `--sandbox`, example reader), #788 (a verifier that mutates the integration tree), and issues #800 (`startsWith("..")` containment sites) and #807. Each is to be fixed or carried here as a known limitation at the RC.

## Not in this release (unless it merges before the cut)

BG-3 firing (#812 in flight); MT-2 slices 3-4; SB-1 further slices; HK-1 events other than `pre-tool` and `post-tool`; HK-2 git-URL installs and trigger-loaded skills; PA-4 qualification of transient delegation and TUI/sidecar exposure of `/goal` and `/loop` (not verified); PA-3 live-gateway and interrupted-effect reconciliation; an npm package (D13); macOS and Windows.

|---|---|

| Workspace plugin approval, migration | `docs/PLUGINS.md`; #798 #808 #810; `cli/test/plugin_trust.test.ts` |
| Project hook allowlist, verified copies | `docs/HOOKS.md`; #782 #805 |
| `mcp.allow` name semantics | `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md`; #778 #783 |
| Unattended verifier, UTC, 5-minute floor, missed runs | `docs/SCHEDULES.md`; #799 #801 #802; `cli/test/schedule_*.test.ts` |
| `--listen` socket | `docs/PROTOCOL.md` "Socket transport"; #797; `cli/test/sidecar_socket.test.ts` |
| Goal pause, protected state, token cap | `docs/v1.3.0/PA3_GOAL_LIFECYCLE.md`, `PA3_ACCEPTANCE.md`; #806 #809 #811 |
| Trigger trust model | `docs/TRIGGERS.md`; #803 |
| ACP conformance | `docs/evidence/AC2_ACP_CONFORMANCE.md`; #749 |
| VR-2, VR-3 | `docs/evidence/v1.3.0/VR2.md`, `docs/evidence/VR3_SANDBOX_DENIALS.md`; #756 #745 |
| Unit table, review record, gates, open items | [`v1.3.0-READINESS.md`](v1.3.0-READINESS.md) |
